results.question: how long do i keep tax records
results.answer:
**How long to keep tax records?**  

The IRS says you must keep records for as long as they may be needed to administer any part of the tax law. In practice that means:

| Type of record | How long to keep it | Source |
|----------------|---------------------|--------|
| General income and deduction records (e.g., receipts, invoices, bank statements) | Until the period‑of‑limitations ends for the tax year on which the claim was made. The timing of that period depends on what you’re claiming – but the rule is “keep it until the period of limitations lapses.” | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| Employment‑tax records (payroll, FICA, etc.) | At least **4 years** after the date the tax became due or was paid (whichever is later). | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| Property and asset records (depreciation, basis, sale of assets) | Until the period‑of‑limitations ends for the year in which you dispose of the property in a taxable disposition. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |

**Why the extra “until the limitations end”?**  
The period‑of‑limitations is how long the IRS can still assess additional tax or how long you can amend your return for a refund or credit. Storing the supporting documents gives you proof if the IRS asks later.  

**If a record is no longer needed for tax purposes**  
Don’t throw it away right away. Check whether insurers, creditors, or other parties require you to keep it for longer. The IRS only sets the minimum; other parties might need the documents for longer. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  

> **Bottom line:** Keep your tax‑related documents in a safe place and delete them only when you’re certain the IRS and any other required parties no longer need them. The exact time depends on what the record supports, but all general income/deduction records are held until their specific limitations period expires. Employment‑tax records stay for 4 years, and asset records stay until the ownership or sale of that asset has a limitation period that ends.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

results.question: why do i need to keep business records
results.answer:
You need to keep business records for several practical and legal reasons:

1. **Tax compliance** – The IRS requires that you keep books that clearly show your income and expenses for each tax year. These books and the supporting documents (receipts, invoices, deposit slips, etc.) let you prove the numbers you report on your tax return. Without them you could not prove that the amounts you claim are true, and you might face penalties if the IRS suspects you under‑reported income or over‑claimed deductions.  
   *[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)*

2. **Audit defense** – If the IRS or another tax authority inspects your return, they will want to see the records that support every line item. Having a complete, organized set of records speeds up the examination and makes it easier for you to explain any items that are questioned.  
   *[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)*

3. **Business management** – Good records let you see how much money is coming in, where you’re spending it, and what your profits are. This information helps you make informed decisions, prepare financial statements (income statement and balance sheet), and seek loans or investment.  
   *[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)*

4. **Legal and regulatory requirements** – Other authorities (e.g., OSHA, employment‑tax agencies) also require you to keep certain records for specific periods. Keeping these records protects you from legal or regulatory penalties.  
   *[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)*

5. **Reconciling bank accounts and preventing errors** – By recording transactions daily and reconciling your checking account each month, you can catch mistakes in deposits or withdrawals before they become big problems.  
   *[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)*

**Bottom line:** Keeping thorough, accurate business records is essential to meet tax laws, defend against audits, manage your company’s finances, and comply with other regulations. They are the evidence that the money you earn and spend is legitimate, and they help you run your business more effectively.

results.question: how do i check my workplace for hazards
results.answer:
To check your workplace for hazards you can follow a step‑by‑step process that is based on the Practical Safety & Health Handbook for small businesses.

1. **Set up a safety and health program** so everyone knows hazards are a priority.  
   *The handbook lists the core elements of a program – reporting procedures, worker training, daily conversations, and worker involvement in inspection and control.* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=9)

2. **Use a self‑inspection checklist**.  
   *The handbook includes industry‑wide checklists that help you spot potential problems in your specific work areas.  Work through each checklist, checking off items that are “Yes” for each hazard.* [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

3. **Gather supporting information** while inspecting.  
   *Collect injury and illness records, training logs, maintenance logs, and incident reports.  Combine this data with the checklist results to see where you have challenges.* [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

4. **Pay special attention to key hazard categories** that the handbook highlights:

   * **Walking‑working surfaces** – make sure walkways are clear, guards are in place, and fall protection is used on raised work surfaces.  Review the specific checklist for walkways and elevated surfaces.  Check that hazard signs are posted and that access/egress is safe.  The handbook provides a checklist with these items and links to OSHA standards.  (See Section Walkways and Section Walking‑Working Surfaces.) [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=79)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=73)  
   * **Confined spaces** – identify any permit‑required confined spaces, post danger signs, have a written program, ensure proper ventilation, test the atmosphere, lock out hazardous energy, and provide attendants and communication.  The checklist shows each step that must be “Yes.”  Reviewing this list will let you see whether your workplace meets the required controls. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=66)[[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=67)  
   * **Housekeeping & ventilation** – maintain clear space around electrical panels, control dusts and vapors with ventilation, keep exits clear, and follow sanitation guidelines. [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=12)

5. **Involve workers in the inspection**.  
   *Workers can help identify hazards, suggest controls, and even take responsibility for implementing those controls.  This is encouraged in the handbook’s safety program checklist.* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=9)

6. **Use the resources linked in the handbook**.  
   *If you find you need help, the On‑Site Consultation Program offers a free, confidential visit from trained OSHA consultants.  That program can audit your whole site or focus on a particular concern and will help you implement controls and improve your program.* [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=90)

7. **Document and follow up**.  
   *After each inspection record the items checked, any corrective actions taken, and verify that controls remain effective over time.  The handbook says inspections should be routine, so repeat them regularly.* [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

**Summary of steps**  
1. Put on a safety/health program.  
2. Run a self‑inspection using the handbook checklists.  
3. Collect workers’ reports and existing records.  
4. Focus on walkways, confined spaces, and housekeeping.  
5. Involve workers in finding and fixing hazards.  
6. Ask for a free OSHA On‑Site Consultation if needed.  
7. Document findings and verify controls continually.

Following these steps will help you identify, control, and monitor workplace hazards so you can keep your employees safe.

results.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
results.answer:
**Cash vs. Accrual Accounting – the short answer**

|  | Cash method | Accrual method |
|---|---|---|
| **When you record income** | When money actually comes in. | When you earn the money, even if you haven’t received it yet. |
| **When you record expenses** | When you pay the money. | When the expense is incurred (when the service or product is delivered or used), even if you haven’t paid yet. |
| **Key rule** | Income = money received, Expense = money paid. | Income = money earned, Expense = money spent (or incurred). |

---

### Why the difference matters

1. **Income timing**  
   * **Cash**: You report a payment the year you receive it.  
   * **Accrual**: You report an advance payment only if the advance is received and the tax year ends, or you may postpone it only to the next year. If you postpone it further, you can’t. In general, the income is recognized when the tax liability is fixed and the economic performance has occurred. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)

2. **Expense timing**  
   * **Cash**: An expense is deductible only when you actually pay it.  
   * **Accrual**: You can deduct an expense when **both** (a) the liability is fixed and (b) the economic performance has happened. For example, if you buy office supplies in December, receive them, and pay the bill in January, you can still deduct the expense in the year you received the supplies (2025) because the liability was fixed and it was economically performed that year. If the supplies are an ordinary recurring expense, you can deduct them even if they are delivered later. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)

3. **Inventory rules**  
   * If you buy, produce, or sell merchandise, you normally **must** use the accrual method for inventory and for sales of that inventory. Small businesses can sometimes choose not to keep inventory records, but they still need a method that reflects income. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)

4. **Special situations**  
   * **Related‑person payments**: Under the cash method, you can’t deduct an expense to a related person until you actually make the payment and that amount becomes part of the related person’s gross income. The rule keeps the cash method consistent. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)

5. **Canceled debt (a trick test case)**  
   * If a creditor forgives part of your debt, a cash‑method taxpayer does **not** include that forgiven amount in income because the payment would have been a deductible expense.  
   * An accrual‑method taxpayer **does** include the forgiven debt in income because the expense was already deductible when the debt was incurred. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=23)

---

### Quick cheat‑sheet

| What you’re looking at | Do you report it now, when it’s paid, or when it’s earned? |
|---|---|
| **Cash received** | **Cash** (now) vs. **Accrual** (when earned) |
| **Bill received** | **Cash** (now) vs. **Accrual** (when financially obligated) |
| **Goods delivered** | **Cash** (when paid) vs. **Accrual** (when delivered) |
| **Refund forgiven** | **Cash** (not income) vs. **Accrual** (income) |

If you’re unsure which method you’re using, look at when you actually receive money versus when you actually earn it. The examples above show how the two methods handle the same transactions differently.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 15)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)

results.question: can i deduct business travel
results.answer:
Yes – you can deduct the ordinary and necessary costs that you incur while traveling for business.  The deduction is available on your federal return (for example, on Schedule C for a sole proprietor) and is subject to several rules that limit what can be taken and how much.  Here’s a quick overview of the key points you need to know:

| What you can deduct | How it works | Where to find the rule |
|---------------------|--------------|------------------------|
| **Transportation** (air, train, bus, car, taxi, limousine, tolls, parking) |  You can take the cost of getting from your “tax home” to your business destination and back, plus any transport between the airport/rail station, hotel, and work site.  | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Car or truck use** |  If you use your vehicle, you may either (a) use actual business expenses (gas, repair, insurance, etc.) or (b) use the standard mileage rate.  You cannot claim both. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40), [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=37) |
| **Lodging** |  Hotels, motels, and other overnight accommodations are fully deductible when the trip is overnight or long enough that you need sleep or rest to perform your duties.  | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Meals** |  Generally 50 % of the cost of meals is deductible when the trip is overnight or qualifies as a “long enough” trip.  You can use actual expenses or the standard meal allowance provided by the IRS.  | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Other incidentals** |  Phone calls, fax use, dry‑cleaning, and tips paid for lodging or meals are deductible at 100 % when they are business‑related. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Reimbursement of employees** |  If you pay an employee for travel and meals, the amount you reimburse can be deductible, but how it is reported depends on whether you use an accountable or non‑accountable plan. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |

### How to decide if a trip counts

1. **Away from your tax home:** Your “tax home” is the city or general area where your business is located.  You are traveling away from home if:
   * Your duties require you to be outside that area for a significant part of a day, **and**
   * You need sleep or rest to carry out your work while away. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)

2. **Business use only:** If the trip has a personal component, you can only deduct the portion that is strictly for business.  (See the flower‑shop example: only the 80 % of vehicle expenses that were for deliveries were deductible.) | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=36)

3. **Document it:** Keep receipts for transportation, lodging, meals, and other expenses.  Note the purpose of each expense so you can prove it was business. | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=2)

### Quick checklist

- **Transportation (tax home → destination → home)** – Yes  
- **Vehicle operating costs** – Yes, if you use actual expenses or the standard mileage rate, but not both.  
- **Lodging** – Yes, if overnight or long enough for rest.  
- **Meals** – 50 % deductible (or use the standard allowance).  
- **Phone, fax, cleaning, tips** – 100 % if business‑related.  
- **Employee reimbursements** – Deductible, but note the plan type.  
- **Personal portions** – Not deductible.  

If you meet the “away‑from‑home” test and the expense is ordinary and necessary for your trade or business, you can claim it.  For full detail or special situations (e.g., standard mileage vs. actual expenses, accountable plans, or how to treat fuel taxes), refer to the IRS publications mentioned above (Pub. 463, Pub. 15,Pub. 334, etc.).

results.question: how do i describe my target market
results.answer:
**Describing your target market**

1. **Define the niche**  
   • *Who* is “your best customer?” Identify the specific group of people or businesses that will buy your product or service. This is the *target market* (the “market niche”) you will focus on.  
   • You can classify it in two main ways:  
     - **Business markets** – by industry, company size, location, product use or application.  
     - **Consumer (household) markets** – by demographics (age, gender), geography, economic status, lifestyle or the benefits the product gives them. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

2. **Describe the customer’s characteristics**  
   • For each segment, list clear details such as:  
     - Age range, gender, income level, education, job title or industry (for B2B).  
     - Where they live or work (city, suburb, rural).  
     - Lifestyle habits, interests, values that relate to your product.  
   • This helps you create a picture of the typical buyer so you can speak to them directly in your marketing mix.  

3. **Estimate size and growth potential**  
   • Use data from census, industry reports, sales tax info or similar sources to get a ball‑park number of people or firms in that niche.  
   • Show how the total market is expected to grow over the next few years and estimate what portion you can realistically capture. This gives investors a sense of the business’s market opportunity.  
   • Keep it simple: “We estimate a 5‑year growth of X% and aim to capture 2% of the market.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

4. **Why this market matters to you**  
   • Explain why these customers are the best fit for what you offer—maybe they have a pain point your product solves or they value a feature you provide.  
   • This justification shows you understand the relationship between your product and the customers’ needs, reinforcing the idea that you’re targeting the right group. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

5. **Use examples**  
   • *Retail*: “Our target market is health‑conscious teens (ages 13‑18) who live in urban areas and want convenient, protein‑rich snacks.”  
   • *B2B*: “Small marketing agencies (fewer than 20 employees) in the Northeast that need affordable, cloud‑based project‑management tools.”  
   These concrete examples demonstrate how you applied the segmentation criteria and sizing steps.

**In short**:  
1. Pick the niche.  
2. Outline who those customers really are (demographics, geography, behavior, etc.).  
3. Size the niche and show growth.  
4. State why they’re the right fit for your product.  
5. Support it with data or clear examples.

That’s the recipe for a clear, actionable target‑market description—drawing directly from the guidance in Segment 3.

results.answer:
**Are you exempt from OSHA injury‑recordkeeping?**

You may be exempt if **both** of these conditions are true:

| Condition | What it means |
|-----------|---------------|
| **Small business** | You had only **10 or fewer workers** at **every time** during the entire last calendar year. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14) |
| **Low‑hazard industry** | Your business is in one of the industries listed in **29 CFR 1904 Part B Appendix A**, which are considered low‑hazard. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14) |

If you meet either of those conditions, you are **partially exempt** from keeping OSHA logs (Form 300, 301, and 300A). However, **you still must report**:

* any **fatalities**,
* any **in‑patient hospitalizations**, **amputations**, or **loss of an eye**

to OSHA within the required time limits (8 hrs for a fatality, 24 hrs otherwise). | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

---

### When you’re not exempt

If you **do not** meet the above exemption criteria, you **must** keep and possibly submit the injury/illness records:

* For establishments with **250 or more workers** (or 20‑249 workers in certain high‑hazard industries), you must **electronically submit** Form 300A each year by March 2. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)  
* If you have **100 or more workers** in designated high‑hazard industries, you must also submit Forms 300 and 301 electronically by March 2. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)  
* All injury/illness records (Forms 300, 300A, and 301) **must be kept on site for at least five years**. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)

---

**Bottom line:**  
- **Yes, you could be exempt** if you are a very small business (≤10 workers all year) **or** in a low‑hazard industry.  
- **No, you’re not exempt** if you have more than 10 workers, are not in a low‑hazard industry, or do not meet the specific exemption criteria. In that case you must keep and, for larger or high‑hazard workplaces, electronically submit the required OSHA injury/illness records.

results.question: how do i start a business and keep my taxes organized
results.answer:
**How to start a business and keep your taxes organized**

---

### 1. Pick a legal structure  
Decide if you’ll be a sole proprietor, a partnership, an LLC, or a corporation (C‑corp or S‑corp).  
Each structure has different filing rules and requires a unique taxpayer‑identification number – usually an Employer Identification Number (EIN) if you’re any type of business other than a single‑person sole proprietorship using your Social Security number.  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)

---

### 2. Get a taxpayer‑identification number (TIN)  
* **SSN** – Use for sole‑prop owners who are U.S. citizens or permanent residents.  
* **ITIN** – For non‑resident aliens who can’t get an SSN.  
* **EIN** – Required for partnerships, corporations, and most LLCs; also needed for sole‑prop owners who have employees or payroll taxes.  
You can obtain an EIN online, by fax, or by mail.  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)

---

### 3. Choose an accounting method  
* **Cash method** – Record revenue when you receive it and expenses when you pay them.  
* **Accrual method** – Record revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, even if cash hasn’t changed hands.  
Pick the method that best shows the real income of your business, and stick with it each tax year.  
[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)

---

### 4. Set up a simple bookkeeping system  
1. **Separate books for each business** if you run more than one.  
2. **Use a checkbook or accounting software** that records all transactions.  
3. Keep a **summary** (“journal” and “ledger”) that lists gross income, deductions, and credits.  
4. Maintain **supporting documents**—sales slips, invoices, receipt books, bank deposit slips, canceled checks—to prove each entry. Organize them by year and type of income/expense.  
[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

---

### 5. Keep electronic records  
An electronic storage system (e‑filing, cloud backup, accounting software) must:
* Index, store, preserve, and retrieve records accurately.  
* Produce legible copies for the IRS when needed.  
* Be tested to show it meets IRS requirements.  
You may destroy hard copies once you have a compliant electronic backup.  
[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)

---

### 6. Record keeping fundamentals  
* **Income statements** (show profits or losses for a period).  
* **Balance sheets** (assets, liabilities, and equity on a specific date).  
* Separate business receipts from personal or non‑business income.  
* Keep receipts for *deductible* expenses as soon as they happen.  
These records both help you manage the business and satisfy the IRS.  
[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

---

### 7. File and pay taxes on time  
* Use the tax‑calendars (Pub. 509) to know due dates for quarterly estimated taxes, payroll taxes, and final returns.  
* Forms you might need: 1040 (and schedules), Schedule C (sole‑prop profit/loss), Schedule SE (self‑employment tax), W‑2/W‑3 (payroll), 1099‑NEC (non‑employee payments), and any special business‑tax forms (e.g., 1128 for changing tax classification).  
* Pay taxes electronically when possible; the IRS lists many benefits for e‑filing.  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=1)

---

### 8. Stay compliant and avoid penalties  
* Retain all business records for at least **seven years** (or longer if specific items require it).  
* Keep copies of all entries and reports in case the IRS requests inspection.  
* If your electronic system fails, maintain original hard copies until you prove the system meets IRS standards.  
[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=2)

---

### 9. When in doubt, get help  
* The IRS offers free small‑business resources (Pub. 583, Pub. 505, etc.).  
* The SBA and local chambers of commerce can advise on best practices.  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=1)

---

**Bottom line:**  
1. Pick your business type and get the right TIN.  
2. Choose a clear accounting method and set up separate, accurate records.  
3. Keep both paper and electronic backups for at least seven years.  
4. File all required forms on schedule, paying any taxes due promptly.  
5. Use IRS resources or professionals when you’re unsure.  

Sticking to these steps keeps your records tidy and helps you avoid surprises when the IRS comes to check.

results.answer:
**How to keep your employees safe and your premises accessible**

| What you need to do | Why it matters | Where it’s in the handbook |
|---------------------|----------------|---------------------------|
| **Make sure only trained attendants work in permit‑required confined spaces** – they must know how to handle an emergency and have the right Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) and respiratory gear. | If someone falls in, the right gear and training can mean life or death. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=68) |
| **Quick‑exit routes and rescue gear** – provide a clear way to pull workers out and have lifelines, retrieval equipment, and rescue teams ready. | Speed can prevent serious injury or drowning. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=68) |
| **Verify communication and rescue services before entry** and keep the confined space free of gas, flammable vapors, or toxic air. | A warning system and clear air detect problems early. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=68) |
| **Have a written program** that lists all confined spaces, the hazard‑control steps you’ll use, and who is in charge. | Documentation keeps everyone on the same page and shows you’re following OSHA rules. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=66) |
| **Keep walkways free of hazards** – repair cracks, loose boards, or other dangers before people use them again. | A broken step can cause a slip or fall. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=79) |
| **Give workers a safe way to reach walk–working surfaces** – use ramps, handrails, or steps that are marked and stable. | Workers should be able to move around the shop or office without tripping. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=79) |
| **Make sure you have enough exits** – each floor should have no fewer than the required number of doors based on how many people you have. | In an emergency, people need a fast, clear way out. | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=28) |
| **Mark every exit clearly** – use “EXIT” signs that are at least 6 inches tall, with lettering at least ¾ inch wide, and put them on the door and along the path to the door. | People can find the way out even in the dark or chaos. | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=28) |
| **Keep exit doors unobstructed** – never lock, block, or jam them while the building is occupied. | A stuck door can hold people in a fire or other danger. | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=23) |
| **Install panic or fire‑exit hardware** on required exit doors so they can be opened with about 15 lb of force. | Workers can pull the door open quickly in an emergency. | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=23) |
| **Provide a ramp or other accessible entrance** – use a ramp that is no steeper than 1:12, at least 36 inches wide, and has railings or edge protection if there’s a drop‑off. | People with wheelchairs, strollers, or luggage can enter the building safely. | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11) |
| **If a ramp isn’t feasible, offer an alternative service** (home delivery, take‑out, curb‑side pickup, or a place to order for a clerk to bring outside). | This keeps people with mobility needs able to buy your product or use your service. | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11) |
| **Protect workers on surfaces higher than 4 ft** – use guardrails, safety nets, or personal fall‑protect devices; keep objects from falling by using toeboards or canopies. | Falls from height are one of the most common serious workplace injuries. | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=73) |
| **Store materials on elevated surfaces in a way that can’t tip or collapse** and provide a head‑room clearance. | A falling load can crush or knock a worker. | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=73) |
| **Test emergency lighting at least once a month for 30 sec, and once a year for 90 min**. | In a power outage or fire, lighting keeps exit paths visible. | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=28) |

---

### Quick checklist

1. Train attendants and keep rescue gear ready – **Seg 1**  
2. Write and follow a confined‑space program – **Seg 2**  
3. Repair walkways and provide clear pathways – **Seg 3**  
4. Verify enough exits, clear signs, and functional exit doors – **Seg 5, 9**  
5. Add a ramp or other accessible entrance and offer alternates if not possible – **Seg 6**  
6. Guard elevated work surfaces and keep material stored safely – **Seg 8**  
7. Test emergency lights monthly – **Seg 5**  

Following these steps uses the information in the handbook to create a safer, more accessible workplace. If you’re missing any of the items above, that part of the plan needs to be developed or updated.

## 1. Writing a Business Plan  
A business plan is a written map of how your company will operate, market itself, grow and stay profitable.

3. **Attach the numbers later** – financial tables can be added after the narrative.  
4. **Review, revise, get feedback** – ask a mentor, accountant or business counselor to read it.  

*If a section doesn’t fit your business, skip it or replace it with something more relevant.*

---

## 2. Setting Up Accounting (Recordkeeping)  

### Choose an Accounting Method  
- Pick a method that clearly shows your taxable income for the year (cash or accrual).  
- For each separate business, keep a separate set of books.  
- Corporations must also keep board‑meeting minutes.  
[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)

### Build a Record‑Keeping System  
| Feature | What it does | How to set it up |
|---------|--------------|------------------|
| **Business Checkbook** | Primary source of entries | Keep it orderly; every cheques, deposits, and withdrawals recorded |
| **Journals & Ledgers** | Summarize transactions (gross income, deductions, credits) | Write each transaction into the appropriate journal, then post to the ledger |
| **Supporting Documents** | Proof of every entry | Store sales slips, invoices, receipts, deposit slips, canceled checks, etc. |
| **Electronic Storage** | Modern alternative to hard copies | Must index, preserve, retrieve, and reproduce in legible format; IRS can test it | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12) |

### Keep the Core Records

- **Gross Receipts** – keep receipts for every source of money (cash register tapes, deposit slips, receipt books).  
- **Deductible Expenses** – record right when they occur to avoid forgetting.

These help you and lenders gauge business health.

**Do you need an EIN?**  
- **Yes, if you meet either of the following conditions:**  
  1. You pay wages to one or more employees.  
  2. You file a pension or excise‑tax return.  
  In either case the IRS requires a separate Employer Identification Number (EIN) to be used as your taxpayer identification number (TIN).  
  If you are a sole proprietorship with no employees and you are not filing pension or excise tax returns, you can use your Social Security Number (SSN) instead of an EIN on most returns [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6).

- **How to get one:**  
  - Apply online at IRS.gov/EIN (immediate issuance).  
  - Or file Form SS‑4 by mail/fax, or call 267‑941‑1099 for international applicants [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4).

---

**What accounting method comes with an EIN?**  
- Having an EIN does **not** dictate a particular accounting method.  
- For businesses, you can choose either the **cash method** or the **accrual method**, depending on what best reflects your income and expenses and complies with IRS rules.  
- The choice of method is independent of whether you have an EIN; you must simply consistently apply the method you select [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=28)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).

| Need an EIN? | Why? | How to Apply |
|-------------|------|--------------|
| ✔ | Pay employees or file pension/excise taxes | Online IRS site, Form SS‑4, or telephone for international |
| ✖ | Sole proprietor, no employees, and not filing the above returns | Use SSN on Schedule C |

| Accounting Method | Options | Note |
|--------------------|---------|------|
| Cash | Records revenue when received and expenses when paid | Simple for small businesses |
| Accrual | Records revenue when earned and expenses when incurred | More complex, required in some situations |

If you’re unsure which method to choose, the IRS provides guidance in Pub. 538 and Pub. 334, or you can consult a tax professional.

results.question: what forms do i keep for injuries and how long do i keep them
results.answer:
**What injury‑record forms must you keep?**  
- **OSHA Form 300** – Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses  
- **OSHA Form 301** – Injury and Illness Incident Report (a supplementary record for each recordable event)  
- **OSHA Form 300A** – Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses (prepared at the end of each calendar year)  

These are the official OSHA forms that a covered employer must create for any injury or illness that is *recordable* (i.e., not just a minor first‑aid case).  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

**How long do you have to keep them?**  
- The OSHA Form 300, Form 301, and Form 300A files must be kept on the worksite for **at least five (5) years**.  
- Worker medical and exposure records (for example, blood‑borne pathogen evaluations, post‑exposure follow‑ups, etc.) should be retained for the period required by the specific type of record, but the basic OSHA injury/illness documents themselves stay for five years.  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)

**Why the five‑year rule matters**  
The five‑year retention period is the minimum OSHA requires so that, if you are inspected or if an injury is later investigated, the records are still available. If your business is subject to OSHA’s injury/illness record‑keeping rules (most businesses with ≥10 workers or in certain higher‑hazard industries), you must keep those records in case of an audit or compliance review.

---

**Quick recap**

| What to keep | How long to keep | Where to keep |
| --- | --- | --- |
| OSHA Form 300 Log | 5 years | On site |
| OSHA Form 301 Incident Report | 5 years | On site |
| OSHA Form 300A Summary | 5 years | On site |
| Worker medical/exposure records | As required by type | On site (or otherwise as specified) |

Stick to the five‑year minimum for the OSHA logs and incident reports, and follow any extra timelines that apply to medical or exposure documents. This keeps you compliant with OSHA’s record‑keeping rules.
